Disparate

dis-PAIR-it — stress on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Disparate describes things or people that are so different from one another that they have little in common.

The festival united disparate crowds — farmers, gamers, and opera fans alike.

Worked Example

The conference brought together disparate professionals—venture capitalists sat next to environmental conservationists, tech entrepreneurs alongside jazz musicians and poets.

Disparate captures not just difference but extreme difference. Plain 'different' is too weak; disparate emphasizes how little these groups overlap or share in common.

How Disparate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

varied

varied: including many different kinds or forms

distinct

distinct: clearly separate and different from others

heterogeneous

heterogeneous: made up of very unlike parts

Antonyms

homogeneous

homogeneous: made up of parts that are alike

uniform

uniform: exactly the same in every case

How Strong Is It? — similar → different → distinct → disparate

similar vs. disparate

similar vs. disparate: Similar sits at the opposite end of the scale from disparate: similar things share obvious common ground, while disparate things have almost nothing in common.

different vs. disparate

different vs. disparate: Different is far milder than disparate — different things merely vary in some way, but disparate things are so unlike that they barely belong in the same conversation.

distinct vs. disparate

distinct vs. disparate: Distinct is stronger than different but still weaker than disparate: distinct things are clearly separate, while disparate things are so fundamentally unlike that comparing them feels strange.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: apart, in different directions (Latin)

Root — par

Root — par: to prepare, make ready (Latin parare) (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: adjective-forming ending: 'having been (made so)' (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Dis- ('apart') + par ('to prepare, arrange') built the Latin verb disparare, 'to separate' — and the look-alike Latin word dispar, 'unequal,' colored its meaning. So disparate things are set apart: too unequal and unlike to have much in common.

Use the root in a new word: separate

Use the root in a new word: separate: Separate comes from the same Latin root parare: to separate things is to arrange them apart, just as disparate things stand apart with little in common.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Disparate is the word for extreme difference—not just different, but so different that the groups or things have little in common. For milder differences, different or distinct works better. Use disparate when you want to stress how little things overlap.
